# Numbers 29: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I couldn't find:** I didn't reach any netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org pages on this chapter, so there are no modern-scholarship or Orthodox notes. For Catholic views I have only Haydock's older commentary on biblehub. I also found no clear case where Protestant traditions disagree on this chapter. The notes below say which tradition each writer belongs to only where that seems useful. Nothing turned up on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. The one debated popular modern teaching I found is the link between the Feast of Trumpets and the rapture (v. 1).

---

**vv. 1–6: Feast of Trumpets**

**v. 1:**
- **Which month:** JFB says the seventh month of the religious calendar was the first month of the civil year, corresponding to our September. It adds that the law gave New Year's Day a religious character by tying it to solemn observances. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-29.html)
- **Gill:** The month is Tishri, a month famous for days to be religiously observed, having more of them in it than any other month in the year. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-1.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** The month fell between harvest and seed-time. His lesson is that the more free time we have from daily work, the more of it we should give to God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-1.htm)
- **Which trumpet:** Guzik quotes a writer saying this feast later became Rosh Hashanah, and that the trumpet here was the shophar, the ram's horn, rather than the silver trumpet of Numbers 10. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)
- **A call to repent:** Precept Austin quotes Edersheim: one main purpose of the shofar was to rouse men to repentance. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-29-commentary)
- **Older Protestant application:** The Biblical Illustrator says the ritual itself was ended by Christ's coming. Believers are now to be "spiritual trumpets" and wake themselves up to think of God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/numbers-29.html)
- **Debated popular teaching (the rapture):**
  - GotQuestions says many believe this day points to the Rapture of the Church. It notes that the rapture is tied to a trumpet in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15. (https://www.gotquestions.org/Jewish-feasts.html)
  - Guzik says some think it would fit for God to gather His people on the Feast of Trumpets itself. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/)
  - A Gospel Coalition essay shows that evangelicals disagree about whether the rapture is a separate event from the Second Coming or happens at the same time. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-rapture-question/)

**vv. 2–4:**
- **What was offered:** Keil and Delitzsch describe the offering as one bullock, one ram and seven yearling lambs, plus grain and drink offerings and a he-goat as a sin offering. All of this came "besides" the monthly and daily offerings. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-1.htm)
- **Each offering's meaning:** Biblehub's study notes say burnt offerings mean total surrender, sin offerings mean cleansing, and grain and drink offerings mean thanks for God's provision. (https://biblehub.com/numbers/29.htm)
- **Fulfilled in Christ:** Bell's commentary says the theme is God's delight in Christ!, because Christ fulfilled each of these offerings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/numbers-29.html)

**v. 5:**
- **JFB:** The feast was described earlier in Leviticus, but here the burnt offering is spelled out in more detail, and in addition to it, a sin offering is prescribed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-29.html)
- **Barnes:** This day's special offering looked ahead to the offering of the great Day of Atonement. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-1.htm)

**v. 6:**
- **Guzik:** The feast's offerings did not replace the daily or monthly ones. Special obligations did not replace normal obligations; they were added to them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The day was "doubly solemn." As a new moon it required the monthly sacrifices, and as a holiday it required extra victims on top of the regular burnt offerings. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/29.htm)

---

**vv. 7–11: Day of Atonement**

**v. 7:**
- **Ellicott:** The full law for this day is in Leviticus 16 and 23. The "affliction" seems to have included fasting, although the word which denotes fasting is not employed, nor is there any express injunction respecting fasting in the Pentateuch. (https://biblehub.com/numbers/29-7.htm)
- **Gill:** The people afflicted their bodies by fasting and their souls by repentance. He notes that Acts 27:9 calls the day "the Fast." (https://biblehub.com/numbers/29-7.htm)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The phrase is an expression which denoted fasting; cf. Numbers 30:13, Psalm 35:13, Isaiah 58:3. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-7.htm)
- **Guzik:** Afflicting the soul showed humility and repentance. It also linked the worshipper with the suffering sacrifice, even as the believer identifies with Jesus Christ on the cross. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)

**vv. 8–10:**
- **Ellicott:** These sacrifices were the same as those for the first day of the month. They were offered in addition to the atonement sin offerings of Leviticus 16 and the daily burnt offerings. (https://biblehub.com/numbers/29-7.htm)

**v. 11:**
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Another sin offering is added besides the goat, to match the people's affliction. For the acknowledgment of guilt would have been a dreadful torment to their consciences without the hope of reconciliation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/29-7.html)
- **Matthew Henry, on our repentance:** Even our repentance has faults that need atoning for: we must repent that we have not repented better. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_029.cfm)
- **Matthew Henry, on the old sacrifices:** The extra sin offering also shows that the old sacrifices could not take sin away, which Christ has done. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_029.cfm)

---

**vv. 12–34: Feast of Tabernacles, days one to seven**

**v. 12:**
- **Matthew Henry:** The joyful Feast of Tabernacles came soon after the Day of Atonement, for those that sow in tears shall soon reap in joy. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_029.cfm)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The people did not stop all work for the seven days. Instead they lived in tents and performed what was required each day. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/29.htm)

**vv. 13–16:**
- **Gill:** Counting the sin offering and the daily lambs, there were no less than thirty two animals sacrificed on this day. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-32.htm)
- **Why so much was required:** Precept Austin quotes Bishop Patrick. The cost was easier to bear at this season because barns and winepresses were full. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62404/)

**vv. 17–34: why the number of bulls drops each day (13 down to 7)**

Several explanations are given:
- **Fewer sins, or the Law fading away (Gill):** The drop may show the people's sins decreasing, or rather the gradual waxing old and vanishing away of the ceremonial law. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-32.htm)
- **Calvin's note:** It quotes Scott's guess that the Mosaic system would gradually wax old, and at length vanish away when the promised Messiah came. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/29-12.html)
- **Barnes:** He thinks the numbers were simply arranged to land on seven on the seventh day. He mentions, without endorsing it, the view that the Law's fading into the Gospel is hinted at here. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/29-12.html)
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** The aim was to reach the holy number seven on the last day. The drop also shows the feast's festive character gradually lessening. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-32.htm)
- **Trapp (quoted by Guzik):** As their sins decreased, so should the sacrifices, or it may picture the legal offerings wearing away. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)
- **Matthew Henry:** God may have been allowing for human weakness, since people tend to resent the cost of religion. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_029.cfm)
- **Kelly (Brethren):** The pattern shows that devotion will not stay as strong as it was at first. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/29-12.html)
- **Seventy bulls for seventy nations:**
  - Precept Austin reports that Jewish teachers linked the total of 70 bulls to the 70 nations of the world. In their view, one fewer each day meant those nations would dwindle until all was under the Messiah. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-29-commentary)
  - Biblehub's notes connect the 70 to the nations of Genesis 10 and say Israel's worship has worldwide implications. (https://biblehub.com/numbers/29.htm)

**v. 18 (and vv. 21, 24, 27, 30, 33), "according to the number prescribed":**
- **JFB:** This means following the ritual order God had already set for grain and drink offerings. (https://biblehub.com/library/jamieson/commentary_critical_and_explanatory_on_the_whole_bible/nu_29_1-40_the_offering_at.htm)

**v. 19 (and the repeated sin offering):**
- **Matthew Henry:** Every day had a sin offering. Our burnt-offerings of praise cannot be accepted of God, unless we have an interest in the great sacrifice which Christ offered. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-39.htm)
- **Matthew Henry, on daily routine:** Repeating the same services every day is no burden to God if done from the heart. The daily offering was never dropped: No extraordinary services should jostle out our stated devotions. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_029.cfm)

**v. 32:**
- **Barnes:** The stress on seven, the covenant number, hints that the harvest blessings came through God's covenant. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-32.htm)

---

**vv. 35–38: The eighth day**

**v. 35:**
- **Ellicott:** Ellicott offers "closing feast day" as an alternative reading. He says the main idea of the Hebrew word is restraint—i.e., from the performance of servile work. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-35.htm)
- **Cambridge Bible:** The Hebrew word ʿatzereth does not itself mean the gathering was especially solemn. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-35.htm)
- **Gill:** The eighth day was not really part of the feast but a sort of appendage to it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-35.htm)
- **Clarke (Methodist):** The Jews saw this as the high day of the feast. It was on this day that our blessed Lord called the Jews from the letter to the spirit of the law (John 7:37). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/numbers-29.html)
- **Water-pouring rite:** Guzik describes a first-century ritual in which water from Siloam was poured on the altar. He says Jesus used this picture to teach about Himself. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The eighth day was more solemn than the days just before it, but less solemn than the first. Quoting Du Hamel, Haydock says it was called the feast of "retention," because the people stayed near the tabernacle. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/numbers/29.htm)

**vv. 36–38:**
- **Ellicott:** The eighth-day sacrifices were the same as those for the Feast of Trumpets and the Day of Atonement. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-35.htm)
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** The month therefore ended with the same sacrifices that began it, so the Day of Atonement left its mark on the whole month. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-35.htm)
- **Guzik's quoted source:** The eighth day had the fewest sacrifices, to teach them not to trust to the multitude of their sacrifices, nor to expect remission of sins from them, but from the one and only sacrifice of Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)

---

**v. 39: vows and freewill offerings**
- **Ellicott:** The required sacrifices were offered separately from anything given to fulfil a vow or as a freewill gift. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-39.htm)
- **Gill:** "Set feasts" is better read as "appointed times," since one of these days, the Day of Atonement, was a fast and not a feast. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-39.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "These things shall ye do" can mean "sacrifice." It compares the Greek wording to Luke 22:19. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-39.htm)
- **Benson:** The many sacrifices show that removing sin is not such trivial things as many would make them, but matters of infinite moment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/29-39.htm)
- **Pett:** This verse shows that making vows belonged to Israel's ongoing pattern of dedication. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/numbers-29.html)
- **Yearly totals:** JFB counts 1,241 animals a year offered at public expense. Guzik gives "at least" 1,086 lambs, 113 bulls and 32 rams, and says none of it could take away sin. The two counts differ. (https://biblehub.com/library/jamieson/commentary_critical_and_explanatory_on_the_whole_bible/nu_29_1-40_the_offering_at.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)

**v. 40:**
- **Precept Austin:** Moses passed on these laws even though he knew he would never keep these feasts in the land himself. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-29-commentary)
- **Guzik:** Israel was about to enter the land and needed to be reminded that sacrifice was central. As part of the Sinai covenant, it could not be ignored. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-29/)
